Sexual health

Practice bringing up STI testing and responding when a partner is willing to talk or feels questioned. Keep the focus on your needs and a shared conversation.

You can ask a health question and keep your boundary. Honest conversation can include uncertainty, more information, and time to decide.

Why this topic can feel awkward · Read the guide

A common concern

“Will they think I don't trust them?”

An example of a question you might have.

A health conversation can begin with honesty

You can acknowledge that a topic feels awkward and still bring it up. Saying 'I'm nervous asking' or explaining that testing matters to your comfort can help state your intention clearly. You can ask about testing histories and questions without making assumptions about someone's health based on appearance, identity, or how well you know them.

Make room for questions and a pause

People may have different experiences with testing or may not know which questions to ask. UHS provides information about STI testing and access to care; a clinician can help with individual testing questions. Agreeing to discuss testing is only one part of a conversation about boundaries and protection. You can wait, seek information, or stop if you do not feel ready to continue.

Learning context: Berkeley UHS, SHEP, and PATH to Care.

About this story

Six rounds of opening a health conversation, responding to mistrust, and deciding what can wait.

You are Noah, 22, and your partner Jordan is 23. You are Berkeley students who have been dating for a few weeks. Sitting at a campus cafe, you are discussing weekend plans. You want to talk about STI testing before deciding whether to have sex.

Your homepage settings carry over here. Explore six rounds and a few tiny side quests. Change levels, revisit a choice, or pause at any time. No typing required.
